Budget Reports and Variance: Reading the Monthly Report and Explaining the Gap

Unit 1: Financial Management. Lesson 3 of 60 in CHTM Academy.

On the eighth working day of the month a report appears in your inbox with your cost center at the top. One line is highlighted. Finance wants a written explanation by Friday. This happens every month of your career, and the manager who can read the report and write the explanation in ten minutes is the manager whose budget requests get believed.

What the monthly budget report holds

Five columns, repeated twice: once for the month and once for the year to date.

Account                 Budget     Actual     Variance   Percent
Salaries                 48,000     51,600      (3,600)   (7.5)
Maintenance and repairs  12,000      8,400       3,600     30.0
Purchased maintenance    30,000     30,000           0      0.0
Travel and education      2,000      5,400      (3,400)  (170.0)
Supplies                  1,500      1,350         150     10.0
Total                    93,500     96,750      (3,250)    (3.5)

Brackets are the hospital's way of writing a negative, and on an expense line a negative variance means you spent more than you were given.

The arithmetic

Variance = actual minus budget. Variance percent = variance / budget x 100. On the salaries line above, 51,600 minus 48,000 is a 3,600 overspend, and 3,600 / 48,000 x 100 is 7.5 percent. Accounting usually asks for a written explanation once a month lands 5 or 10 percent off its budget, so know your hospital's trigger.

Favorable and unfavorable

For an expense, under budget is favorable and over budget is unfavorable. For revenue it is the other way round: more revenue than planned is favorable. Over-expenditure is what draws attention, but a large favorable variance is also a question, because it usually means work did not happen.

Timing variances and real variances

A timing variance is a gap that will close by itself. The contract invoice was due in March and arrived in April, so March looks favorable and April looks terrible, while the year to date is exactly on plan. A real variance does not close: a new position filled early, a part price increase, a vendor rate change, a device failing more often than budgeted. Check the year-to-date column before you write anything, because it separates the two for you. Seasonality and one-time events belong in the same reading: scheduled maintenance clusters in some months, and a single large repair can own a month on its own.

Writing the explanation leadership expects

Three sentences, in one order every time: what, why, and what you will do.

  • What: travel and education is 3,400 unfavorable for the month and 1,100 unfavorable year to date.
  • Why: two technicians attended the school negotiated into the purchase of the new system, which was scheduled this month rather than spread across the year.
  • What you will do: no further school spending is planned before the fourth quarter, so the line returns to plan by year end; the alternative was vendor labor at a higher rate.

Never explain a variance with the word "overspent" and nothing else, and never promise a recovery you cannot show in the numbers.

Forecasting the year end

Divide the year-to-date actual by the months elapsed to get a monthly run rate, multiply by twelve, then adjust for what you know is coming: a contract renewal with an escalation, a vacancy you expect to fill, an irregular part due on its interval. A forecast you carry to leadership in month six is a request for help; the same number discovered in month twelve is a failure.

Exam tip: variance is actual minus budget, and percent is variance divided by budget. On expenses, under is favorable and over is unfavorable. Check year to date before calling a variance real, and write every explanation as what, why, and what you will do.
Remember
Variance is actual minus budget and its percent is variance over budget, read against the year to date so a timing gap is never mistaken for a real one, then explained as what, why, and what you will do.
Deeper explanation

Budget Reports and Variance: Reading the Monthly Report and Explaining the Gap, explained slowly

A full monthly variance report, read line by line

This is period 6 of a twelve-month fiscal year, so half the year has elapsed. Brackets are negatives, and on an expense line a negative variance means overspending.

                        ---------- Month 6 ----------    ------- Year to date -------
Account              Budget   Actual   Var      Pct      Budget   Actual     Var
Salaries             48,000   51,600  (3,600)  (7.5)    288,000  299,400  (11,400)
Overtime              2,000    5,100  (3,100) (155.0)    12,000   24,800  (12,800)
Employee benefits    13,500   15,100  (1,600) (11.9)     81,000   87,500   (6,500)
Maintenance/repairs  12,000    8,400   3,600   30.0      72,000   58,900   13,100
Purchased maint.     30,000   30,000       0    0.0     180,000  180,000        0
Travel/education      2,000    5,400  (3,400)(170.0)     12,000   13,100   (1,100)
Supplies              1,500    1,350     150   10.0       9,000    8,600      400
Total                109,000  116,950 (7,950)  (7.3)    654,000  672,300  (18,300)

Which of these is a real variance

Line                 Reading                                 Real or timing
Salaries             over in the month and over year to       real: a position was
                     date by about 4%                         filled earlier than planned
Overtime             double the budget twice over             real, and the most
                                                              serious line on the page
Employee benefits    tracks salaries, because it is a rate    real, and follows from
                     applied to them                          the two lines above
Maintenance/repairs  favorable in the month and 18% favorable timing in part, real in
                     year to date                             part: see below
Purchased maint.     exactly on budget, as a contract paid    neither; verify it was
                     in equal installments should be           invoiced, not assumed
Travel/education     wildly over in the month, barely over    timing: school seats
                     year to date                              negotiated into a purchase
Supplies             small and favorable                      ignore it

The maintenance and repairs line deserves a second look precisely because it is favorable. A department 18 percent under its parts budget at the half year is either buying better or not doing the work. Check the completion rate and the backlog before you report it as good news, because the favorable parts line and the unfavorable overtime line may be the same story: too few people, so scheduled maintenance slipped and the hours that were worked were paid at premium rates.

The written explanation, as leadership should receive it

Salaries, overtime, and benefits: $30,700 unfavorable year to date. The approved second technician position was filled in month two rather than month six, and the vacancy it replaced was covered on overtime for the five months before that. Overtime also carries the coverage for one technician on extended leave. Scheduled maintenance completion has held at target, which is what the overtime bought.

Action. Overtime returns to budget from month seven with the new technician productive, and the leave coverage ends in month nine. The year-end forecast is $1,335,600 against a $1,308,000 annual budget, a 2.1 percent overage carried almost entirely by overtime already incurred. I will report again at month nine before requesting any amendment.

Forecasting the year end from this page

Step                                        Arithmetic              Result
Year-to-date actual                         672,300                 672,300
Months elapsed                              6
Monthly run rate                            672,300 / 6             112,050
Straight projection to twelve months        112,050 x 12          1,344,600
Less overtime correction from month 7       (2,100 x 6)            (12,600)
Plus known contract escalation in month 9   (900 x 4)                3,600
Adjusted forecast                                                 1,335,600
Annual budget                                                     1,308,000
Forecast variance                                                   (27,600)

The straight projection and the adjusted forecast differ by $9,000, and the adjustments are the part leadership can actually act on. State them.

What to memorize

Variance          actual minus budget
Variance percent  variance / budget x 100
Favorable         expenses under budget, revenue over budget
Unfavorable       expenses over budget, revenue under budget
Explanation       usually required once a line is 5% or 10% off budget
Timing variance   closes by itself; check the year-to-date column
Explanation shape what, why, what you will do
Forecast          year-to-date actual / months elapsed x 12, then adjust
